title: Topgolf saved over $11.3 million after leaving VMware
gist: Topgolf moved 12,000 VMs off VMware to VergeIO's VergeOS after Broadcom's pricing changes would have raised costs 400 percent, reporting over $11.3 million saved. The case shows VMware competitors winning migrations that bundle hardware refreshes, with tenancy and integrations as key factors.

insights.claim: Topgolf faced a 400 percent increase in VMware costs under Broadcom and moved 12,000 VMs to VergeIO's VergeOS, reducing or eliminating over $11.3 million in combined infrastructure costs.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Concrete savings evidence that Broadcom's pricing is pushing large customers to alternatives.
insights.quote: Overall, we reduced or eliminated over $11.3 [million] in combined infrastructure costs
insights.locator: Topgolf's VMware costs were going to increase

insights.claim: Topgolf replaced 650 VxRail hosts with about 400 Dell PowerEdge servers in six months, cutting hardware spend 87 percent and software costs 77 percent, and secured a five-year ELA versus a reported three-year VMware offer.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Hardware consolidation plus the contract term shows the switch yields leverage on both costs and commitment length.

insights.claim: Savings have partly eroded because compute and storage hardware prices have risen in the market, though Topgolf says they remain large.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Rising hardware costs reduce the savings of migrations that pair with refreshes.
insights.quote: we have taken a hit to the original numbers, but it's still exponential

insights.claim: Topgolf says the $11 million-scale savings are not typical because its needs are larger, but VergeIO says avoiding licensing, proprietary HCI appliances and separate tools for data protection and multi-site management is common.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Adjust for scale before extrapolating, but the three savings levers recur across migrations.

insights.claim: VergeIO gets about 70 new customers per quarter, most coming off VMware, typically at renewal, hardware refresh, many-site deployments or multi-tenancy needs.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Triggers like renewals and refreshes show where VMware churn will concentrate.

insights.claim: Topgolf picked VergeOS mainly for tenancy; it says VMware could not segregate clusters into tenants, and even SDDC Manager could not manage its number of vCenter instances.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant management at scale is a functional weakness competitors can exploit beyond price.
insights.quote: VMware lacks the ability to segregate clusters into tenants, which has made it a nightmare to manage at scale.

insights.claim: Most migrations are bundled with hardware refresh or modernization, and the hard part is scheduling all of it; Topgolf also replaced game panels, rewired columns and moved to Kubernetes gaming architecture.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Migration projects expand in scope, lengthening sales cycles and driving adjacent hardware spend.

insights.claim: Third-party integration gaps are the most common friction: Topgolf lost Rubrik compatibility, used VergeIO snapshotting and pivoted to Veeam for threat hunting and ransomware protection.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Ecosystem maturity is VMware's remaining moat, and backup vendors like Veeam can gain.
insights.quote: Integration is the most common friction point, and it shows up after the migration.
insights.locator: As Topgolf reduced its use of VMware

insights.claim: API-first design and early Terraform and Ansible support meant Topgolf did not need to retool its infrastructure-as-code.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: IaC compatibility lowers switching costs, a requirement for VMware alternatives.
